segments.text: Hey guys, in this lesson I will  cover AWS CodePipeline. So,
what is CodePipeline? CodePipeline is a  service that we can use for creating CI/CD
pipelines. It's a continuous delivery  service, so when we're using continuous
integration and continuous delivery  or continuous deployment, this is the
service that helps us to bring everything  together and create the automated pipeline.
So, we have an AWS CodePipeline. Within the  pipeline, we create stages. For example,
a stage could be a source code stage for our  GitHub repository. It could be a build and
test stage for building and testing our code,  and that might use AWS CodeBuild as the service
that we integrate. But it doesn't have to  be CodeBuild. It doesn't have to be AWS;
there are other options as well.  And then for the deployment,
here we're using CodeDeploy. So, this is to  deploy the code out to the actual application.
So, we have a CodePipeline. Within  that, we can create our build,
test, and deploy phases for whatever release  process it is that we want to implement. So,
when there are code changes, how do we want  those to go through the various stages of
being synchronized into a repository, pushed  through to a build and test service, tested,
and then ultimately out to the end application,  perhaps with some manual approval stages
or some other kind of approval actually  happening as part of the pipeline as well?
So, here we've got GitHub as the source code,  CodeBuild for doing the build and test, then we've
got a manual approval step, and then CodeDeploy  to push through to the running application. So,
the developer commits the code to the repository,  the code is then pushed through to CodeBuild,
so CodePipeline is causing that event trigger  to happen. Then it goes to manual approval. So,
now you could actually have someone checking  and approving it at the right time, after
it's actually passed the relevant human checks as  well as the automated checks that happen through
CodeBuild. So, we have an approver approving  the updates, and then they're pushed through
CodeDeploy, which actually deploys the actual  updates to the code out to the application.
So, what are the possible integrations? There  are lots of different AWS and third-party
integrations for the various different stages in  a pipeline. For instance, for the source stage,
we can have our code in S3, in ECR, in  GitHub, in GitLab, in Bitbucket, and more.
For the build stage, we can actually run  shell commands or we can use CodeBuild,
ECR, or Jenkins. For test: CodeBuild, Device Farm,  Jenkins, Ghost Inspector, UI Testing, Micro Focus,
StormRunner, Load, RunScope, API Monitoring,  and this list changes from time to time,
so it may not be accurate. When we get into the  actual console, you'll be able to see what the
current integrations are at the time of you  going in and actually building your pipeline.
For the deployment stage, we've  got a variety of options as well:
AppConfig, CloudFormation, CodeDeploy, ECS,  Elastic Beanstalk, AWS Service Catalog, S3,
and Alexa Skills Kit at this particular time.
So, let's cover some of the concepts. We have  pipelines; this is a workflow that describes
how software changes go through the release  process. Each pipeline is made up of a series
of stages. There are two types of pipeline you  can create: a V1 type pipeline, which has a JSON
structure and contains standard pipeline stage  and action-level parameters, and then the V2 type,
which has some additional options for  release safety and trigger configuration.
We have artifacts as well. So, these are the files  or changes that are being worked on by the actions
and stages in the pipeline. Each pipeline stage  can create its own artifacts. They are passed
and stored in S3 and then passed on to the next  stage. Examples might include your source code,
your built applications, dependencies,  definition files, templates, and more.
Then we have stages. So, pipelines are  broken up into stages. For example, source:
that is our source code repository where our  code changes are committed. Then we have build,
where our changes are built. So, that can  mean, for example, compiling our code,
and it can also mean running some tests on  the code as well. Then we've got stages,
so the code is deployed and tested in  a staging environment, for example,
and we might add that stage before we go  through to deployment to actual production. So,
we can build our own customized pipelines  depending on our specific requirements. Each
stage can have sequential actions and/or parallel  actions, and for example, our stages would be:
Source, Build, Test, Deploy, Low Test, etc. We  can also define manual approval at any stage.
Another concept is actions. Stages contain  at least one action, such as a source
action from a code change, where a developer is  committing a change of the code to the code base,
or an action for deploying the actual  application to instances. Actions can
affect artifacts and will have their own  artifacts as either input or output, or both.
Transitions are the progress from one  stage to another inside of a pipeline.
Pipeline executions are the actual execution  of a set of changes released by a pipeline,
and each has its own unique ID. So, here,  for example, an execution would be where
the developer committed the code,  pushed it through to the repository.
That change has then triggered the pipeline, so  that will create an execution of the pipeline.
That execution may be that the entire pipeline  is used, so the code ends up being deployed
right out to the actual application, or maybe  it fails, or maybe it results in the developer
getting some feedback that they need to make  some changes because the build and test phase
didn't actually complete successfully. All  of those would still be executions. So,
an execution corresponds to a set of changes,  such as a merged commit or a manual release of
the latest commit. Two executions can release the  same set of changes at different times as well.
So, to summarize: CodePipeline gives us  a way to integrate various different AWS
and third-party services that represent the  different stages of the release process and
create the relevant automations between  one stage and another. And here's just
an example of some of the options that we've  discussed earlier in terms of the different
AWS and third-party services that you  can integrate into different stages.
So, in this lesson, we're going to create a  pipeline using AWS CodePipeline and an application
running on AWS Elastic Beanstalk. So, the lab  will look a bit like this: We've got GitHub,
and that's going to be included in a CodePipeline  as the source stage, and the deployment stage
here is actually using Elastic Beanstalk. So,  Beanstalk can be its own deployment provider
within a CodePipeline. Now, our developer can  actually push code to the GitHub repository,
and the CodePipeline will then trigger  the update via Elastic Beanstalk to make
updates to the actual live application.  So, let's head over and build this out.
The first thing we'll do is  head over to Elastic Beanstalk,
and we're going to create an environment.  It's going to be a web server environment,
and I'm going to call this  "DevOps Labs." Scroll down,
it's going to create the environment name for me.  For platform type, we'll choose managed platform,
we'll choose Node.js, scroll down, we'll use the  sample application for now, and click on "Next."
There's quite a lot of pages in the new wizard.  Depending on whether you've used Beanstalk before,
it may or may not have the service role.  If you've not used Beanstalk before,
you might have to create a new  service role. If you do that,
it's going to create one of this name. If you  have used Beanstalk before, you've probably
already been through that process, so  you can use the existing service role.
Now, you are required to do a few things here that  I don't even need to do. One is to add a key pair,
so I'm just going to add any one. I  also need to add an instance profile,
even though I don't want to supply permissions  to any other services, but it will error if we
don't. So, I'll just choose one of the  instance profiles I already have in my account.
Click on "Next." I'm going to choose the default  VPC. I can choose one or two subnets within my
default VPC. Don't need a database. Click on  "Next." Leave the defaults. Uh, don't need to
have any special monitoring. So, let me just see,  is there any changes I want to make here? Uh,
I can leave these defaults. In fact, I'll just  choose my web access group. Scroll down. Click on
"Next." Basic monitoring is fine. Turn off managed  updates. We don't need any of this at the moment.
I'm just trying to make sure that it doesn't error  because the new Beanstalk wizard, and it's not
really new, but it's been around for a while,  but it's kind of, uh, it has a lot of settings
which it doesn't really tell you, but that are  actually prerequisites for it to actually complete
correctly. So, hopefully, that will do the job.  Let's submit, and it is launching the environment.
So, while that's launching, I'm going to head  over to CodePipeline, so we'll get ahead of
ourselves a little bit here. And under "Settings"  and "Connections," we're going to use a repository
in GitHub. Now, in order to be able to do that,  you need to create a connection. You only actually
need one. I've actually done this a couple of  times, so I can delete that one. And what you need
to do here is just click on "Create connection,"  choose GitHub, give it a name, and then click on
"Connect to GitHub." When you do that, it should  require authentication. Because I'm already
authenticated, it might not show that right now.  Okay, so I actually don't need to set any settings
there, literally just click on "Connect," and it's  going to create that connection. Now, again, for
you, that's probably going to require you to log  into GitHub. I'm actually already logged in here.
Plus, I've done this before, so I only need one  of these, so I'll just delete the extra one. So,
that means we now have authentication so that  we can set our repository as the source stage.
So, I'm going to click on "New" in GitHub, and  I'm going to create a repo called "Develop Dlabs
Public Repository," and then click on "Create."  So, that's done. Let's just come back and check
our Beanstalk environment. Still being created.  Let's click on the option here just to see. It's
not ready quite yet. So, while that's happening,  what I'm going to do is open up AWS CloudShell,
and we're going to use CloudShell for the Git  client. So, what I can do is come back to the
repository, click on this option to copy  the clone link, let's come to CloudShell,
clear my screen, and I'm going to git clone paste  in that URL, and now we've got our repository. So,
I should now be able to change into DevOps Labs.  There we go. Let's come back to our environment
here. It says it's launched. Let's check it out.  There we go. It is launched, and it's launched.
You can see that it's got this, uh, sort of  splash screen that they provide, the default page,
green on the left, and I know that because we're  going to change that shortly as part of an update.
So, what I want to do now is come back  to CodePipeline. We're going to click on
"Pipelines" here on the left-hand side, click  on "Create pipeline," choose "Build custom
pipeline." I'm going to give it the name "DevOps  Dlabs," allow it to create a new service role,
click on "Next." For "Source provider," I'm  going to choose GitHub via GitHub App. I
should now be able to select my connection  that I created a little bit earlier on,
and now I'm going to go and find the DevOps  Dlabs here. For "Default Branch," we're going
to enter "Main," and then we're going to click on  "Next." We don't have a build stage at this time,
we're not going to use a testing stage,  so now we just skip through until we see
"Deploy." And what we can do here is select  Beanstalk. Input artifact should be "Source
Artifact." Application name should be "DevOps  Labs," and environment name is "DevOps Labs
ENV." Click on "Next." Let's scroll all the way  down, and we're going to create our pipeline.
So, the pipeline is created, and we're going to  see it's initially going to kick off the pipeline.
So, it's triggering it based on the source stage.  So, it's going to check with GitHub: is there any
code there to deploy? And I'm expecting that to  error, and that's because there isn't any code
to deploy at this stage. That's fine, no problem  at all. We're going to add the code in right now.
So, what you want to do is head over to  CloudShell in AWS CloudShell. I'm going
to click on "Actions," "Upload file," and  from the AWS Developer Tools of the course,
download "Select Node.js Blue.zip." I've got  the file. Let's unzip, and that's created a
directory. And now I'm going to copy all of the  files from Node.js Blue to the DevOps folder.
Change back to DevOps, just clear my screen, run  ls, and now we have these various different files,
including an index.html. Now, the difference  with this index.html is that it actually
specifies that the color on the left-hand side  of the index.html is blue rather than green.
Okay, so these are the changes. Now I can run git  add -A, git commit -m "Added updated index.html
and other files as well." But that's okay. And  then we're going to push this change up to the
repository. Enter my username and then enter  my password, and that's pushed the change.
So, let's go back now and watch what happens here  in our pipeline. And you can see straight away we
have "In Progress" for our source stage. So, the  change which we've just pushed up to our GitHub
repository—here we can see all these different  files—has triggered the pipeline, and now it's
triggered through to the deploy phase, where  Beanstalk is going to be making this change. So,
if we head back over to Beanstalk here, we can  see that the environment is now being updated. So,
it won't be instant, but fairly quickly, we're  going to find that this changes to blue. So,
you can watch the progress here, and really within  a minute or two, I suspect it should be ready.
So, the environment update was successful.  Let's now come back and refresh the screen here,
and sure enough, our background has changed  to blue. So, that's an example of pushing code
via GitHub through a code pipeline with  the deployment provider being Beanstalk,
and it's actually updating our  environment and making that change.
